question: On 3 December 2025 it was revealed that Hamas interfered with EU funding in Gaza. In 2022, the Commission ceased funding to the Islamic University of Gaza, given the university’s affiliation with Hamas. In 2019, the EU introduced a clause in its contracts with non-governmental organisations (NGOs) stipulating that beneficiaries must not be affiliated with or transfer aid to EU-listed terrorist groups or entities.

In response, Palestinian NGOs refused to sign it and launched the ‘Palestinian National Campaign to Reject Conditional Funding’. In response to the 7 December 2023 review, the Commission conducted a review of EU funding to Palestine and noted that ‘the review confirmed the safeguards in place are effective’. 1.
How does the Commission explain the persistent failure of EU safeguards to prevent funds from reaching EU-designated Palestinian terrorist groups, persons and affiliates?

Why did the EU’s 2023 review not reveal that Hamas required EU-funded NGOs to cooperate with them and that they were complicit in hiding Hamas’ abuses in Gaza, and will the Commission initiate a new review?

Will the Commission cease funding NGOs operating in Palestine, where corruption and links to terrorist entities are rife, and will it adopt stricter due diligence standards to protect EU taxpayers’ money?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.3.2026) The Commission implements rigorous safeguards to ensure that no persons or entities receive EU funding if these are involved in any criminal or unethical practices, including terrorist financing and offences. Those safeguards include ex-ante and ex-post risk assessment, monitoring and strong controls and audits.

Currently, the Commission does not possess any substantiated information that would highlight that any of its partners are not complying with EU standards and due diligence processes. Following Hamas’ terrorist attacks against Israel on 7 October 2023, the EU carried out a thorough review of EU financial assistance for Palestine1.

The review’s objective was to ensure that no EU funding indirectly enabled any terrorist organisation to carry out attacks against Israel, to assess the feasibility of projects in the changed circumstances, to ensure full respect for EU legislation and policy and to prevent the possible abuse of EU funding to incite hatred and violence.

The review showed that the Commission’s controls and existing safeguards in place work well, and no evidence has been found to date that money has been diverted for unintended purposes. A new review of the entire development assistance of the EU for Palestine is not envisaged.

The Commission took note of the reporting of alleged interference of Hamas in the EUfunded activities of international non-governmental organisations in Gaza. The Commission takes any allegations regarding EU-funded partners seriously. It has specifically asked the Israeli authorities to share documents or any form of evidence that would help the EU to correctly assess these allegations.

Should there be clear evidence that its partners are not complying with EU standards and due diligence, the Commission will take all the appropriate measures, such as the suspension or early termination of contracts and/or the recovery of the funds disbursed. Furthermore, it could lose its eligibility for future EU funding.
1 *This designation shall not be construed as recognition of a State of Palestine and is without prejudice to the
individual positions of EU Member States on this issue.
